title: Psalm 35: Contend with My Opponents, O LORD
summary: A man falsely accused and repaid evil for good asks the LORD to fight for him like a warrior and plead his case like an advocate. Three times he describes his enemies, asks God to act, and promises praise. He recalls how he mourned when his accusers were sick, only to have them gloat when he stumbled, and he ends by asking that those who favor his cause rejoice while he proclaims God's righteousness all day long.
story: Psalm 34 promised that the LORD delivers the righteous from all their troubles. Psalm 35 shows what it feels like to wait for that deliverance while slanderers circle. It is a lament of an individual, and one of the psalms often called imprecatory, because it asks God to bring ruin on enemies. It belongs to the Davidic laments of Book I, and it mixes the language of the battlefield with the language of the courtroom. Its phrase about being hated without reason is picked up in the Gospel of John, where Jesus applies the words of the Psalms to the hatred he met.
historical:
The heading simply says Of David. No event is named. Readers who connect the psalm with David's life often think of his years as a fugitive from Saul, when David had served Saul faithfully and was repaid with suspicion and pursuit (1 Samuel 18 to 26), or of Absalom's revolt, when trusted counselors turned on him. Others see in it the prayer of any Israelite facing a false lawsuit in the town gate. As with other headings, scholars differ on whether it records authorship or places the psalm in a collection associated with David.

What stands behind the psalm is a real feature of Israelite life: accusation before the elders, where witnesses could make or break a case. The law required two or three witnesses and punished false witnesses with the penalty they had tried to bring on the accused (Deuteronomy 19:15-19). The psalm's prayer that the enemies fall into their own net expresses that same principle of justice.
cultural:
Two worlds meet in the psalm. The first is war. The shield and buckler of verse 2 were a large body shield and a smaller hand shield, and the spear and javelin of verse 3 were the weapons of close fighting. God is pictured as a warrior arming for battle on the psalmist's behalf. The second world is the court. Contend in verse 1 translates a verb used for bringing a legal case, and verses 11, 23, and 24 speak of hostile witnesses, a defense, and vindication. In ancient Israel the gate of the town served as its courtroom, where elders heard disputes.

Verses 13 and 14 describe mourning customs: wearing sackcloth, fasting, walking bowed down as one would for a close relative. The psalmist had done this for his accusers when they were sick, which makes their betrayal sharper. The gnashing of teeth in verse 16 was a gesture of contempt and rage, and the cry Aha, aha in verse 21 was the triumphant jeer of those who think they have caught someone at last. Chaff in the wind (verse 5) comes from the threshing floor, where grain was thrown into the air so the breeze would carry away the husks.
literary: The psalm has three sections, each ending in a vow of praise: verses 1 to 10 end with all my bones exclaiming Who is like You; verses 11 to 18 end with thanks in the great assembly; and verses 19 to 28 end with the tongue proclaiming God's righteousness all day long. The first section is dominated by battle imagery, the second by the story of betrayal, and the third by courtroom language and the enemies' taunts. The angel of the LORD appears twice (verses 5 and 6) as the one who drives the enemies away. Quotation is important: the enemies' words are quoted (verses 21 and 25) and answered by the psalmist's words and finally by the words of the faithful in verse 27.

outline.t: A call for the LORD to arm himself as warrior
Prayer that the pursuers be driven away and trapped
Vow of praise: who is like the LORD
False witnesses and friends who repay mourning with mockery
How long, O Lord: plea and vow of public thanks
The gloating enemies and a plea for vindication
Joy for those who favor the righteous, and praise all day

doctrines.note: The psalmist does not take revenge; he asks God, the righteous judge, to hear his case and act. The prayers for ruin are appeals for justice placed in God's hands, often in the form that the wicked fall into their own traps.
The psalm shows that anger at injustice can be brought to God in prayer. It is honest about the desire for vindication and about the pain of betrayal, and it keeps returning to praise.
Much of the psalm describes suffering that is undeserved: evil repaid for good, hatred without cause. Scripture gives room for the innocent to name their innocence before God.

words.note: Riv, to contend, often in a legal sense: to bring a case, to plead a cause. The psalm opens with it, asking God to take up the case against those who contend with the psalmist. The prophets use the same word for God's covenant lawsuit against Israel. Here God is asked to act as the advocate of the falsely accused.

Chinnam, without cause, for nothing. It appears in verse 7 (without cause they laid their net) and verse 19 (those who hate me without reason). The word marks the enemies' hatred as gratuitous. Jesus uses the phrase from the Psalms to describe the world's hatred of him in John 15:25.

Mal'ak, messenger or angel. The angel of the LORD appears twice (verses 5 and 6), driving away the enemies like wind scattering chaff. The same figure encamps around the faithful in Psalm 34:7. In the Old Testament he is God's agent of rescue and judgment, sometimes speaking with God's own voice.

christ: In John 15:25 Jesus says that the world's hatred of him fulfills the word written in their Law that they hated him without reason. The line appears in Psalm 35:19 and Psalm 69:4, and interpreters differ on which he had in mind, possibly both. Jesus fits the pattern of the psalm closely: he was repaid evil for good, faced false witnesses at his trial (Mark 14:56-57), and was mocked by those who gloated over him. Yet the Gospels also show a difference. Where the psalmist asks God to turn the enemies back in shame, Jesus prays for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). The New Testament does not cancel the psalm's cry for justice, but it shows Jesus taking the place of the wronged righteous one and entrusting himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

hard.q: How can a follower of Jesus pray for enemies to be ashamed, trapped, and ruined?
hard.a: Psalm 35 is one of several psalms that ask God to bring harm on enemies, and Christians have struggled with them since the early centuries. Some readers conclude that these prayers belong to an older stage of revelation and are superseded by Jesus' command to love enemies. Others point out that the psalmist is not taking revenge but surrendering it, asking God as judge to do justice, which is exactly what the New Testament also commands (Romans 12:19). Still others read the imprecations as honest speech: God invites the wronged to bring their rage to him rather than act on it. Many add that the psalm's enemies are not merely personal rivals but those who oppose God's righteous one, and that Christians pray them in light of the cross, where justice and mercy meet. Each view takes seriously both the psalm's place in Scripture and Jesus' command to bless those who curse.

questions: The psalmist mourned for people who later turned against him. How do you respond when kindness is repaid with harm?
What is the difference between asking God for justice and taking revenge yourself?
Where in the world today do the falsely accused and the poor need an advocate, and what might it look like to stand with them?
